lessons.module: M00 · What Is An App Factory
lessons.title: What An App Is Made Of
lessons.outcome: You can name the four things every app is made of and explain why a factory reuses tested parts.
lessons.body:
Ava is thirteen and helps on Saturdays at The Tidy Paw, a dog grooming salon run by Juno Platt. Juno keeps her bookings on paper cards, and every week a few clients simply do not turn up. Ava wanted to build Juno an app that would fix this. She opened an app builder, stared at the blank page, and stopped. She did not know where to begin. Then she noticed something that changed how she saw it: every app, however big, is made of the same four things. Screens, tables, rules and people. Name those four first, and the blank page stops being blank.

Start with screens. A screen is one page of an app that a person looks at and touches, such as a calendar, a form or a list. For Juno's salon, one screen might show today's bookings. Another might let a client pick a time. A screen does not store anything on its own. It only shows information and collects it. That matters, because a lot of people think the screens are the app. They are only the front window. Behind every screen sits the part that remembers things, and that is where we go next.

Behind the screens sit tables. A table is where an app stores its data, laid out in rows and columns, rather like a spreadsheet. Each row is one thing, such as one booking. Each column is one fact about it, such as the date, the time or the dog's name. Juno's salon would need a table of bookings, a table of clients and a table of free time slots. The plan of all the tables an app needs is called a schema. Get the tables right and the screens are easy to change later. Get them wrong and everything wobbles.

Next come rules. A rule decides who may see something and who may change it. Juno should see all her own clients. A client should see only their own bookings, never anyone else's. If a second salon used the same app, neither salon should ever see the other's data. In this course, a rule that keeps one group's data apart from another's is called a wall. When a wall fails and someone sees data that is not theirs, that is called a leak. A leak is the most serious mistake an app can make, so the factory tests for leaks again and again.

The fourth thing is people. Every app has different kinds of people using it, and each kind needs different screens and different rules. There is the owner who runs the app. There are the businesses that use it, like Juno's salon. There are those businesses' customers, like the dog owners who book a trim. And there is the public: strangers who have not signed in at all. These ideas come back in the four groups of codes you will meet in Stage 0. Knowing exactly who signs in, and who does not, shapes every table and every rule.

So why does this matter? Most apps today are made by hand. Someone starts from a blank page, invents the screens, the tables and the rules from nothing, and makes hundreds of choices along the way. The next app starts from a blank page again. The same mistakes get made twice, and the same safety checks get forgotten twice. Nothing learned on one app is carried to the next. That can work for a single app. It does not work if you want many apps that are all safe, all tested and all built the same careful way.

An app factory takes a different route. Every idea travels the same road, in the same order, with the same checklist at each step. Instead of inventing parts from nothing, the factory reuses tested parts called bricks. There are 101 bricks, kept on 8 shelves, and they are grouped into 9 ready-made bundles called kits, numbered K00-K08. Kit K00 is the floor that every app gets: the basics, the walls between businesses, and the legal and consent parts. When a problem is found on one app, the fix becomes a checklist line, so the next app does not repeat it.

Let us put it together. Ava now has a plan before she builds anything. For Juno's salon she can list the screens: today's bookings and a booking page. She can list the tables: bookings, clients and time slots. She can write the rules: each client sees only their own bookings, and each salon sees only its own clients. And she can name the people: Juno, her clients and the public. That list is the start of every app the factory makes. Next you will see the road an idea travels, its rooms and its gates. First, a recap.

points: Screens Show And Collect Information
Tables Store Data In Rows And Columns
Rules And Walls Decide Who Sees What
recap.why: Name The Four Parts Before You Build Anything

quiz.q: What is a table in an app?
options: Where data is stored in rows and columns
A kind of screen for staff
quiz.why: A table stores the app's data, with one row per thing and one column per fact.

quiz.q: In this course, what is a leak?
options: Someone seeing data that is not theirs
A spelling mistake on a page
quiz.why: A leak happens when a wall fails and a person sees data that belongs to someone else.

quiz.q: What is kit K00?
options: The floor that every app gets
A kit only for big apps
The last kit to be added
quiz.why: K00 is the floor: the basics, the walls between businesses and the legal parts, on every app.

quiz.q: Why is building every app by hand a problem when you want many apps?
options: Lessons from one app are not carried to the next
quiz.why: Each hand-made app starts from a blank page, so the same mistakes and missed checks repeat.

lessons.module: M00 · What Is An App Factory
lessons.title: The Road, Rooms And Gates
lessons.outcome: You can name the 9 stages, describe the 11 rooms and say which gates need a person to decide.
lessons.body:
Sam is fifteen. One weekend he had an idea for a small app to help his gran keep track of her dog's walks and feeding times, and he wanted it finished by Sunday night. So he skipped straight to building. By Sunday it worked, until his cousin signed in and could read his gran's private notes. Sam had wanted speed. What stopped him was a mistake he never checked for. The lesson he took away was simple: an app is safer when it travels a fixed road, with gates where it must stop and prove itself before it moves on.

In the factory, every idea travels the same road of nine stages, numbered 0 to 8. Stage 0 is Idea, where the idea is written down. Stage 1 is Research, where we check whether people need it. Stage 2 is Base, where we pick a starting point. Stage 3 is Features, where we choose what goes in. Stage 4 is Schema, the plan of the tables. Stage 5 is Data, where test accounts are set up. Stage 6 is Prompts, where the app is actually built. Stage 7 is Launch. Stage 8 is Operate, where the live app is watched every day.

Two things make this road easy to follow. First, the money. Stages 0 to 5 cost no build credits at all. Build credits are what the building platform charges each time it writes code. Stage 6, Prompts, is the only stage that spends them, so every check before it is free. Second, the paperwork. Each app has a card, which holds its 20 codes and is never overwritten, and one document organised by stage. Each stage of that document ends with a line saying when it is finished. That line is the test for the stage.

The road runs through rooms. A room is simply where an app sits while it is at a certain stage, so anyone can see at a glance what is happening. There are 11 rooms in all. Six sit on the main road. Reception holds new ideas at Stage 0. Research holds Stages 1, 2 and 3. The Rig holds Stages 4 and 5, where tables and test data are set up. The Reactor holds Stage 6, the paid build. The Runway holds Stage 7, launch. And Radar holds Stage 8, where live apps are watched.

The other five rooms sit beside the road. Recovery holds ideas that were killed or held, so they are kept as evidence and can be looked at again. Reserve holds spare parts, such as bricks and kits from apps that were switched off. The Ready Room is where locked jobs wait for a free building lane. Rescue is for live apps in trouble that need an urgent fix. And Recycle is where a retired app's parts go back onto the shelves. Nothing in the factory is simply thrown away. Even a failure teaches the next app something.

Between the stages sit gates. A gate is a stop point where the app must prove its stage is finished before it may move on. There are 8 gates on the main road. Screen sits between Stages 0 and 1. Merit sits between 1 and 2. Base sits between 2 and 3. Lock sits between 3 and 4. Schema sits between 4 and 5. Invest sits between 5 and 6. Send sits between 6 and 7. Launch sits between 7 and 8. A gate cannot open while any checklist line for its stage is still not done.

Some gates open by themselves when every check passes. Base and Schema are automatic. Invest is automatic when the build is estimated at 1,500 credits or less. At the others, a person decides: Screen, Merit, Lock, Invest when the build is bigger, Send and Launch. Their yes is the only thing that moves the app. Inside some gates sit smaller checks. Slot, inside Invest, makes sure no more than 3 apps are being built at once, with 1 lane kept free for rescues. Leak and Live, inside Launch, prove nothing leaks and the first real sign-in works.

Launch is not the end. A live app goes round a lap, and three lap gates watch it. Trouble is automatic: if an incident is opened on a live app, the app moves to Rescue. Back to Operate is a person's decision, and the question is whether the fix is proved live. Retire is also a person's decision: should the app be switched off and archived? So that is the whole map. Nine stages, 11 rooms, 8 road gates and 3 lap gates, with a person deciding at the moments that matter most. Let us recap before Stage 0.

points: Nine Stages Run From 0 Idea To 8 Operate
Eleven Rooms Show Where Each App Sits
Gates Stop Apps, A Person Decides At Some
recap.why: A Fixed Road Catches Mistakes Before Real People Do

quiz.q: How many stages are on the factory road?
quiz.why: The road has nine stages, from 0 Idea to 8 Operate.

quiz.q: Which is the only stage that spends build credits?
quiz.why: Stage 6 is where the app is built, and it is the only stage that spends build credits.

quiz.q: Which of these gates opens by itself when every check passes?
quiz.why: Schema is an automatic gate, like Base; Lock and Launch always need a person.

quiz.q: What does the Slot check inside Invest make sure of?
options: No more than 3 builds at once, with 1 lane kept for rescues
quiz.why: Slot limits building to 3 apps at once and keeps 1 lane free for rescues.

lessons.title: The Idea Form
lessons.outcome: You can write an idea as a one-line vision, a named payer and a clear pain, and name the four doors ideas come through.
lessons.body:
Isla's aunt, Mara Quill, breeds dogs and holds a dog breeding licence from her local council. Every time the licence comes up for renewal, Mara spends weeks hunting through folders for paperwork. Isla wanted to turn that headache into an app idea. She wrote two full pages of features: reminders, charts, a shop, a chat room. When she showed it to her aunt, Mara could not tell what the app was actually for. Then Isla learned how the factory starts every idea. Not with features, but with three short answers: what it is, who pays, and what hurts.

Every idea begins at Stage 0, called Idea, in a room called Reception. Reception is free: nothing here costs a single build credit. By the end of Stage 0, the idea will have five things. A card, which is its record. A one-line brief. A kill check, which asks whether the idea should stop now. A set of 20 codes that describe how the app handles businesses, people and data. And a data role, which says who is responsible for the personal data. This lesson covers the first part: the Idea Form, and the doors ideas come through.

Ideas can arrive through four doors. The first is the Idea Form, filled in by a person with an idea. The second is called the flip farm: ideas that arrive already attached to an existing template, so they start with a ready-made shape. The third is the AI door, for ideas suggested by an AI tool. The fourth is the client door, for ideas sent in by outside customers, and it is not built yet. The door an idea came through is recorded on its record, so anyone can later see where it started.

Now the form itself. It opens with a short name and a vision. The vision is one line that says what the app is and what it does, with no list of features. Isla rewrote hers: Litterline, a licence and records hub for dog breeders. That is the whole vision. It is short on purpose. A short line can be checked, argued with and changed. Two pages of features cannot. If you cannot say what your app is in one line, the idea is not ready yet, and that is useful to know before any work starts.

Next, the form asks who pays. This means the person or business whose money keeps the app running, not just who uses it. For Litterline, breeders pay. But there is a second answer: dog clubs can resell it under their own name. A reseller is a business that sells the app to its own members with its own name and colours on it. In our example, the fictional club Northvale Canine Society resells Litterline to its breeders. Naming the payer early matters, because a later gate, Lock, will not let an app move on without one.

The third question is pain. The pain is the problem the app removes, written the way the customer would say it. For Litterline, the pain is that licence renewals mean weeks of paper hunting. Notice that this is not a feature. It does not say reminders or charts. It names something that hurts, and that a breeder would recognise straight away. Good pain lines are plain and specific. A vague pain, such as making life easier, cannot be tested. A specific pain can be checked against real customers in Stage 1, Research.

When the form is sent, the factory engine does five things at once. The engine is the script that moves apps along the road. It writes the idea's card. It creates the app's task at Stage 0, or on hold if the data is sensitive. It adds a row to the list of ideas. It suggests a verdict, which is pass, hold or kill. And it suggests a data role. It also checks whether the factory has seen this idea before, and flags it if so. If a form is ever lost, a safety net writes the card on the next check.

The card is the single home of the idea's classification. It is never overwritten. If something changes, a new version is saved beside it, marked v2, then v3, so the history is always there. There is also an optional extra: a one-screen sketch of the idea, using made-up data and no tables, so a person can picture it. It costs nothing. Isla now has a one-line vision, a named payer and a clear pain, instead of two pages of features. Next, the form asks its biggest question: the 20 codes. First, a recap.

points: Start With Vision, Who Pays And Pain
Ideas Arrive Through Four Doors
The Card Is Kept, Never Overwritten
recap.why: Three Short Answers Beat Two Pages Of Features

quiz.q: What three things does the brief on the Idea Form ask for?
options: What it is, who pays and the pain
quiz.why: The one-line brief covers the vision, who pays and the pain.

quiz.q: Which of the four idea doors is not built yet?
quiz.why: The client door, for ideas from outside customers, is not built yet.

quiz.q: What is a reseller?
options: A business that sells the app to its members under its own name
A person who tests the app
quiz.why: A reseller, like Northvale Canine Society, sells the app to its own members with its own name on it.

quiz.q: What happens when a card needs to change?
options: A new version, such as v2, is saved beside it
The idea starts again with a new name
quiz.why: The card is never overwritten, so changes are saved as new versions and the history is kept.

lessons.title: The 20 Codes
lessons.outcome: You can name the 4 code groups, read a code as a word plus a number and say which 6 codes are required.
lessons.body:
Rory is twelve and was helping his sister fill in the Idea Form for Litterline. Everything went smoothly until he reached a list of 20 short questions with odd capital-letter names like TEN, CUST and SEN. He wanted to answer them quickly and move on. But one question asked how many businesses there are and who sits above them, and he had no idea what it meant. Then it clicked. Each code is just one question, answered with a word and a number. And the number tells the factory which walls the app will need.

These questions are called the 20 codes. A code is a short name for one question about how the app handles businesses, people and data. The full set was frozen on 19 Oct 2026, which means it is fixed and every new idea answers the same 20. They sit in 4 groups. Group 1, Businesses, has 6 codes. Group 2, Who Signs In, has 5. Group 3, Customers, has 4. Group 4, Public, has 5. The groups move from the inside of the app outwards: from the businesses at the core to strangers on the internet.

Every answer is a word plus a number. The word is the code, written in capitals. The number is the level, and each code has its own range. For example, TEN (0-6) counts the layers of businesses. A low number means simple. A high number means more layers, and so more care. The answers are written together, like TEN 3 or SEN 1. Most codes also point to a wall, numbered W1 to W8, that will keep data apart. So by answering the codes, you are already deciding which walls the app will need.

Group 1 is Businesses. TEN (0-6) asks how many businesses use the app and who sits above them. Litterline is TEN 3: breeders, with one reseller, Northvale Canine Society, above them. PARENTS (0-3) asks how many parties one business can sit under. DOWN (0-3) asks what a party above may do to the layers below, such as read them. MEET (0-3) asks whether businesses that do not own each other ever meet. POOL (0-3) asks whether anything is worked out across businesses. EXIT (0-3) asks what happens to a business's data when it leaves.

Group 2 is Who Signs In. ROLE (0-2) asks whether all of a business's staff have the same access, or different roles with different access. BELONG (0-2) asks how many businesses one person can belong to. GUEST (0-1) asks whether a business can let an outside person in with a limited view. HELP (0-3) asks whether someone can see the app as another person sees it, for example to give support, and whether that is logged. JOIN (0-2) asks who can create an account: invite only, people with a join link, or anyone who signs in.

Group 3 is Customers. CUST (0-5) asks how far into a business's own customers the app goes. At 0 only staff use it. At 3, customers can write their own data, and at 5 customers sell to each other. Litterline is CUST 3. PRICE (0-3) asks whether everyone pays the same price. SHARE (0-1) asks whether members can share things with each other. SEN (0-3) asks how sensitive the data is: 0 is ordinary, 1 is personal, 2 is health or clinical, and 3 is children. SEN matters a great deal, as the next lesson shows.

Group 4 is Public. VIEW (0-2) asks whether a stranger can read anything without signing in. POST (0-2) asks whether a stranger can put data in without signing in, such as through a contact form. BRAND (0-2) asks whose name is on the screen: none, one brand, or a brand per business. Litterline is BRAND 2, because each reselling club shows its own name. SEND (0-2) asks what the app sends to outside systems the factory does not control. PAY (0-2) asks whether money moves between parties in one chain, such as payouts within that chain.

Do you need all 20 answers on day one? No. Six codes are required, because the factory cannot judge an idea without them: TEN, CUST, SEN, VIEW, POST and PAY. The other 14 may be answered with a question mark, meaning not yet known. That keeps the form honest. A guess dressed up as a fact is worse than an open question, because nobody goes back to check it. The answers go straight onto the card, which is their only home. Rory filled in the six, marked three others as not yet known, and finished. Let us recap.

points: 20 Codes Sit In 4 Groups
Each Answer Is A Word Plus A Number
Six Required, Fourteen May Be Not Yet Known
recap.why: The Codes Decide Which Walls The App Needs

quiz.q: How many groups are the 20 codes sorted into?
quiz.why: The codes sit in 4 groups: Businesses, Who Signs In, Customers and Public.

quiz.q: Which six codes must always be answered?
options: TEN, CUST, SEN, VIEW, POST and PAY
ROLE, JOIN, HELP, GUEST, BELONG and SHARE
PRICE, BRAND, SEND, EXIT, POOL and MEET
quiz.why: The factory cannot judge an idea without TEN, CUST, SEN, VIEW, POST and PAY.

quiz.q: What does SEN 3 mean?
quiz.why: SEN (0-3) runs from ordinary to children, so 3 means the app holds children's data.

quiz.q: What does a question mark mean as an answer to one of the 14 optional codes?
quiz.why: A question mark honestly records that the answer is not yet known.

lessons.title: Kill Check, Verdict And Data Role
lessons.outcome: You can apply the three kill questions, work out the suggested verdict, name the four data roles and explain the Screen gate.
lessons.body:
Leo had an idea he loved: a version of Trimtable that would make one neat printed price list for a grooming salon. He wanted it built straight away. Then it went through the kill check, and one question stopped it. Would people use it once and stop? Honestly, yes. A salon prints its price list once a year and never opens the app again. Leo was disappointed for about a minute. Then he saw the point. The idea had stopped at Stage 0, for free, before a single hour of research or a single credit was spent.

The kill check is three questions, each with a code name. FRAGILE asks: could the app give wrong answers that look right? An app that quietly misreads a record and shows it as fact is dangerous, because nobody notices. ONESHOT asks: would people use it once and stop? NOHOOK asks: is there no reason to come back? An app that nobody returns to cannot stay alive. These three can all be answered from the description alone, which is why they come first. They need no research, no tables and no money at all.

If any one of the three answers is yes, the suggested verdict is KILL. A verdict is the decision recorded for an idea at a check. A killed idea is not deleted. It is kept as evidence, with its reason and the date, and moved to the room called Recovery. That way, if someone suggests the same idea again next year, the factory finds the old record and does not repeat the work. A person still confirms a kill; the engine only suggests it. Stopping a weak idea early is one of the cheapest wins in the whole factory.

The second possible verdict is HOLD. The engine suggests HOLD when SEN, the sensitivity code, is 2 or 3. That means the app would hold health or clinical data, or data about children. These need extra care under data protection law. Before such an idea may move on, a DPIA must be done. A DPIA, or Data Protection Impact Assessment, is a written check of the risks to the people whose data the app will hold, and of how those risks will be reduced. Until it is signed, the idea waits. It is not killed, only paused.

The third verdict is PASS. An idea passes when no kill answer is yes and SEN is below 2, meaning the data is ordinary or personal, but not health and not children. Trimtable, the booking desk for groomers, is a good example. Salons use it every day to book and check appointments, so ONESHOT and NOHOOK are both no. Its records come from what the groomer types in, so FRAGILE is no. Its SEN is 1, because it holds clients' names and contact details. So the engine suggests PASS, and Trimtable moves towards the Screen gate.

Alongside the verdict, the engine suggests a data role. This comes from data protection law and says who is responsible for personal data. A CONTROLLER decides why personal data is used and how. A PROCESSOR handles personal data on behalf of another business, following its instructions. BOTH means the app is a controller for some data and a processor for other data, decided set by set. NONE means the app holds no personal data at all. The role belongs to each relationship, not the whole company, so one app can play different roles for different data.

Why does the role matter so early? Because it picks the duties. Each role brings its own pack of checklist lines that the app must complete later. A controller has duties such as a privacy notice and a route for people to ask for a copy of their data. A processor needs a written agreement with each business whose data it handles. An app marked BOTH gets both packs. Choosing the wrong role at Stage 0 means the wrong duty lines follow the app all the way to launch, so it is checked here, at the very start.

Now the idea reaches its first gate: Screen, between Stage 0 and Stage 1. The question is simple: start work on this idea? A person decides, and their yes also confirms the data role. The factory can let some ideas pass Screen automatically, but never an idea with a kill suggested, an idea seen before, or an idea from the AI or client doors. Those always wait for a person. Once Screen says yes, the idea leaves Reception and enters Research. You now know the whole of Stage 0. Let us recap the three checks.

points: Three Kill Questions: FRAGILE, ONESHOT, NOHOOK
HOLD When SEN (0-3) Is 2 Or More
Data Role: CONTROLLER, PROCESSOR, BOTH Or NONE
recap.why: Stopping A Weak Idea At Stage 0 Costs Nothing

quiz.q: Which kill question asks whether people would use the app once and stop?
quiz.why: ONESHOT asks whether people would use it once and stop.

quiz.q: No kill answer is yes, but SEN is 3. Which verdict does the engine suggest?
quiz.why: SEN 2 or 3 means HOLD until a DPIA is done and signed.

quiz.q: What does a PROCESSOR do?
options: Decides why personal data is used
Sells the app under its own name
Handles personal data on behalf of another business
quiz.why: A processor follows another business's instructions when it handles personal data.

quiz.q: Which idea can never pass the Screen gate automatically?
options: An idea where a kill is suggested
An idea from the Idea Form with no flags
An idea with a short name
quiz.why: Kill-suggested, seen-before, AI and client ideas always wait for a person at Screen.

lessons.title: The Research Sweep
lessons.outcome: You can list the parts of the research sweep and explain why customers' own words come before our own ideas.
lessons.body:
Esme's neighbour runs Hollin Lane Kennels, a boarding kennel. Esme had heard her talk about inspection day, when an inspector checks the kennel's records, and she wanted to build Stayproof, an inspection pack for kennels. She was sure she knew what kennel owners needed: a smart dashboard with charts. But when she read what kennel owners actually wrote online, almost nobody mentioned charts. They wrote about logs scattered everywhere and panic the night before an inspection. Esme's lesson was clear. Research means listening to customers in their own words before you decide anything.

Once an idea passes Screen, it moves to Stage 1, Research, in the room of the same name. Like Stage 0, research is free: no build credits are spent. The goal is to find out whether real people need this app, what they already use, and what rules apply. The very first job is to check what the factory already owns. Earlier cards, research or mockups for the same idea are searched for by name, including old names, and linked to the card. There is no point researching from scratch what was already found last month.

Next comes the competitor sweep. A competitor, or rival, is any product people already use to solve the same problem. The sweep picks 3 to 5 rivals and records their prices and their reviews. The most useful reviews are the 1 and 2 star ones, because they show exactly what breaks and what annoys people. Every source is dated, so anyone can see how fresh it is. For Stayproof, the rivals might be general kennel software, paper record books and spreadsheets. Even a paper notebook counts as a rival, if that is what owners use today.

The sweep then collects customer words. This means 10 exact phrases people use for the pain, and 10 for the result they want, copied from reviews and groups word for word. Their words, not ours. These phrases are used later for headlines, the sales page and the first screens a new user sees. Alongside them comes review mining: every complaint and feature request is quoted with its link and date, then counted by theme. The top ten themes come first. If forty reviews mention lost logs, that matters more than one clever idea of our own.

With rivals and customer words in hand, we build a gap matrix. A gap matrix is a table. Its rows are features, taken from rivals and from what reviews ask for. Its columns are the rivals. Each box is marked to show one of three things: a feature missing everywhere, a feature customers ask for, or a feature done badly, judged by those 1 and 2 star reviews. The matrix ends with the 3 strongest gaps. Those gaps become our edge, meaning the reason a customer would choose this app instead of what they use now.

Next, the market. Market size means roughly how many possible customers there are, and the trend means whether that number is growing or shrinking. Both must come with sources, never guesses. The audience data must also be lawful. That means using public counts, trade bodies, official company records and search trends, and never scraping people's personal details. Scraping means using a program to copy information off web pages in bulk. A factory that broke data rules while researching an app that must follow data rules would be building on sand.

Then comes the rules flag, short for the regulatory flag. A regulation is a law or official rule that a business must follow. The flag records which ones touch this idea, and whether any of them could stop it altogether. This line is done by a person, not a tool, because judging the law needs a human who understands it. For Stayproof, the flag would name the boarding licence rules, such as the England 2018 Regulations. For Litterline, it would name the dog breeding licence rules. The flag does not decide anything yet. It warns the next gate.

Finally, everything is pulled together into an idea code and a rank. The rank scores four things: market, profit, risk and confidence, which is how sure we are of the evidence. A one-page offer draft is also written, describing the dream customer, the pain in their words and what life looks like after. That page is used again at Stage 7 for the sales page. Esme's research turned a charts app into a logs and inspection app that kennel owners actually asked for. Now the research goes to a person at the Merit gate. First, a recap.

points: Check What We Already Own First
Collect Rivals, Reviews And Customers' Exact Words
Gap Matrix, Market, Rules Flag, Then Rank
recap.why: Customers' Own Words Beat Our Own Guesses

quiz.q: Which reviews does the competitor sweep look at most closely?
quiz.why: Low-star reviews show what breaks and what annoys people, which is where the gaps are.

quiz.q: How many exact customer phrases are collected for the pain?
quiz.why: The sweep collects 10 phrases for the pain and 10 for the result, word for word.

quiz.q: What does the gap matrix end with?
quiz.why: The matrix ends with the 3 strongest gaps, which become the app's edge.

quiz.q: Who completes the rules flag?
options: An AI tool on its own
A person, because judging the law needs a human
quiz.why: The regulatory flag is a person's line, because no tool can judge the law.

lessons.title: The Merit Gate
lessons.outcome: You can explain the four Merit verdicts as a decision tree, say why a person decides and describe the DPIA hold.
lessons.body:
Ruby is fourteen and had followed Litterline all the way through research. The rivals were checked, the customer words collected, and the gap matrix was clear. She wanted a quick yes so the building could start. Instead, the verdict came back RESHAPE, with one line: build it for clubs to resell from the very start, not as an extra later. Ruby was annoyed, until she read the reason and saw that it was right. A clear instruction to change one thing was worth far more than a vague yes that would have caused trouble later.

Merit is the gate between Stage 1, Research, and Stage 2, Base. Its question is: is it worth building? Everything from the research sweep is laid in front of the person who decides: the rivals, the customer words, the gap matrix, the market size, the rules flag and the rank. Before Merit can even be asked, every research line must be done, and the research section of the app's document must not say pending. Merit is the last gate before real work on the app begins, so it is the last cheap place to stop.

Why does a person decide here, and not a tool? Because Merit is the regulatory and data protection kill. It asks whether the law, or the way the app handles people's data, makes the idea unsafe or unwise to build. In this factory the person at Merit is trained in law, and the rule books say plainly that no tool substitutes. For an app used by service businesses, the key question is whose data it holds. The engine has a setting that could let Merit pass on its own, but the rule books treat it as a person's decision.

Merit gives one of four verdicts: GO, HOLD, KILL or RESHAPE. They are not a list to pick from at random. They work as a decision tree, which means a short chain of questions asked in order. If the idea is good as it is, the verdict is GO. If not, ask: can you name what to change? If yes, the verdict is RESHAPE. If not, ask: can you name what to wait for? If yes, the verdict is HOLD. If you can name neither, the verdict is KILL. Every verdict is recorded with a date and a reason.

RESHAPE means the idea is worth something, but one part must change first. The idea keeps its id, which is its permanent number, and goes back to Reception to be reworked. Ruby's Litterline verdict was exactly this. HOLD means the idea is fine, but something outside it must happen first, and the verdict names that trigger, such as waiting for a new rule to be published. Simply waiting for a free building lane is not a HOLD. That is a queue, and a queue is not a verdict. Queues are handled later, at the Slot check.

KILL means the idea stops. It burns the id, which means that number is never handed to another idea. At Merit, no parts have been built yet, so a killed idea goes to the room called Recovery, with its reason kept as evidence. It can be looked at again later if something changes. There is another verdict, called RECYCLE, used when an app's parts go back on the shelves, but RECYCLE never applies at Merit. There are no parts to recycle yet. That is part of why stopping here costs so little.

There is one special hold to know about. If SEN, the sensitivity code, is 2 or 3, the app would hold health data or children's data. Such an idea is held until its DPIA, the written risk check, is done and signed, and the card stays on HOLD until then. The factory saves effort here: a base DPIA is written once for the shared core, and each new app built from it adds a one-page add-on. Some rules come with it, such as photos being private by default and children's details never being public.

When the verdict is GO, it must be carried. A verdict given on a screen is not enough. The rule is simple: a move writes, or it did not happen. In the same session, the verdict is written onto the card and into the app register, the list of every app. The app's folder is copied from the factory template, and the idea leaves the board of decisions waiting. Now it is a real app at Stage 2, Base. Litterline went back, was reshaped for clubs, and later came through Merit with a GO. Let us recap.

points: Merit Asks: Is It Worth Building
GO, HOLD, KILL Or RESHAPE, As A Decision Tree
SEN (0-3) At 2 Or More Needs A DPIA
recap.why: A Person Judges The Law Before Anything Is Built

quiz.why: Merit asks whether the idea is worth building, after the research is done.

quiz.q: At Merit you can name exactly what must change. Which verdict fits?
quiz.why: If you can name what to change, the verdict is RESHAPE and the idea goes back to Reception.

quiz.q: Why does RECYCLE never apply at Merit?
options: No parts have been built yet
The card is deleted at Merit
quiz.why: RECYCLE returns parts to the shelves, and at Merit no parts exist yet.

quiz.q: What does the rule "a move writes, or it did not happen" mean?
options: The verdict must be written to the card and register in the same session
The idea must be written twice
Only written ideas can enter Reception
quiz.why: A verdict only counts once it is written into the card and the app register in the same session.

lessons.title: Picking A Base
lessons.outcome: You can explain how the factory picks a base, copies the template and passes the Base gate.
lessons.body:
Meet Rory. He had an idea for a booking desk for dog groomers, a bit like our sample app Trimtable, and it had just passed the Merit gate. He wanted the first screens working by the weekend, so he opened a blank project and started typing. By Sunday he had rebuilt a sign-in page, a menu and a cookie notice, all things he had built before, and not one part that was new. Then it clicked. If you start from a base that already works, you only build the parts that make your app different. That is Stage 2.

Stage 2 in the factory is called Base. A base is the starting app you copy before you add anything new. Stage 2 sits in the Research room, the same room as Stages 1 and 3, and it is free: no build credits are spent here. Credits are the units the build platform charges for each paid building turn. The job of this stage is short and strict. Choose a base, copy the template folder, save a backup, check for duplicates, list the bricks, and prove the base is safe. Then the Base gate opens by itself.

The first choice is remix or rebuild. To remix means to start from an existing base app that the factory already owns, kept on a shelf of bases, and change it. To rebuild means to start fresh, because no base fits. The factory records a fresh start as BESPOKE, which means made to order. A rebuild is never chosen on a whim. It has to come with the result of a dedup check that proved nothing suitable already exists. Most of the time a remix wins, because the floor of the app, meaning sign-in, menus and legal pages, is already built and tested.

Dedup is short for de-duplication, which means removing copies. The dedup check is run live on the build platform, not from memory. It asks a simple question: does something we already own do this job, or most of it? If the answer is yes, that is the base. If an earlier base was looked at and turned down, its name is written down with the reason, so nobody suggests it again next month. This one habit saves a lot of money later, because building the same thing twice costs twice, and the second copy has to be tested and looked after as well.

Next, the factory clones the template app folder. To clone means to make an exact copy. Every app gets its own folder made from the same template, so every app's papers sit in the same places. Be clear about one thing: this is a folder of documents, not the live app. The app itself is created on the build platform later, when the feature list is frozen at the Lock gate. The moment a base is chosen, an Export ZIP is taken. A ZIP is one packed file holding a full copy, so there is always a safe point to go back to.

Then comes the brick list. A brick is one reusable part, such as booking or invoices, and a kit is a named bundle of bricks that ship together. The list includes the kits, by their ids, and every brick's status is quoted word for word, never guessed. One rule from the checklist is worth remembering: never say there are no bricks for something until you have searched the kits and the design notes. The colours are settled here too. They live in one place only, as rows in the app's palette table, never typed into the code. You will meet bricks properly in the next lesson.

A base can look fine and still leak. A leak is when one person or business can see data that belongs to someone else. So the base gets a security vet, which means a careful check, using two separate test accounts. Each account signs in and tries to see the other's records. If either can, the base fails, however good it looks. This matters even more for a reseller app like Litterline, where a club such as Northvale Canine Society sits above many breeders. A copy of a leaky base copies the leak into every app built on it.

Now the gate. The Base gate sits between Stage 2 and Stage 3, and it asks one question: is the base named, and has the vet passed? It is an auto gate, which means no person has to click yes. When every Stage 2 checklist line is ticked, the engine moves the app on by itself. Compare that with Screen and Merit, where a person decides. Base can be automatic because its questions have plain answers: a name is written or it is not, and a test passed or it did not. Let us recap what makes a good base.

points: Remix An Owned Base Or Rebuild As BESPOKE
Dedup Check And Export ZIP Come First
Base Gate Is Auto Once Base Named And Vetted
recap.why: A Proven Base Means Only New Parts Get Built

Start from an existing base the factory owns
quiz.why: To remix is to start from a base app the factory already owns and change it.

options: A dedup check that proved nothing suitable exists
A signed letter from the club

options: The engine, automatically, when every line is done
quiz.why: Base is an auto gate: when every Stage 2 line is done, the engine moves the app on.

quiz.q: Why is an Export ZIP taken as soon as the base is chosen?
options: To keep a safe copy to go back to
quiz.why: The Export ZIP is a full packed copy, so there is always a safe point to return to.

lessons.title: Bricks, Shelves And Kits
lessons.outcome: You can explain what bricks, shelves and kits are, and why K00 sits under every app.
lessons.body:
Isla was planning Litterline, our sample licence and records hub for dog breeders. She sat down and wrote every feature she could think of: dog records, health notes, litters, reminders, forms, invoices. She wanted a full parts list she could trust. An hour later she had sixty loose items, and half of them were the same thing under different names. Bookings, appointments and reservations were all one idea. Then she saw how the factory does it. It picks a few named kits, each a known bundle of parts, and the list is clean in minutes.

A brick is one reusable part of an app that does one job. Booking is a brick. Documents is a brick. Sign on the screen is a brick. Each brick has an id that starts with BR, such as BR-BOOKING, plus a name, the tables it needs and a status. The factory keeps them all in one list called BRICK-REGISTRY, and the version in use, v0.16, holds 101 bricks. A table, by the way, is a grid of rows and columns that stores one kind of record, a bit like one tab in a spreadsheet.

Bricks sit on shelves, and the shelves are sorted on a colour spine, which is a fixed order where each shelf has its own colour. There are 8 shelves. BASICS is the floor: sign-in, menus and basic records. Boundaries holds walls, roles, security and legal. Bucks holds plans, invoices and payment rails. Body holds the parts you see, like booking and records. Brand holds the name, colours, logo and domain for each brand. Boost holds public pages, reviews and funnels. Brains holds scoring, matching and reports. Bots holds reminders, sequences and imports that run on their own.

If you count the registry, the shelves are not even. Body is by far the biggest, with 63 of the 101 bricks. That is partly because the registry folds the Bots shelf into Body: a bot is a way of doing something, not a separate thing, so bot bricks are filed under Body. After Body come Brains with 11, Bucks with 10, Boundaries with 9, Boost with 4, Brand with 3, and BASICS with just one brick, BR-BASICS. You do not need to remember the numbers. Remember that the shelf tells you what kind of job a brick does.

A kit is a named bundle of bricks that ship together, so one idea is picked as one thing with a known cost, not as fifteen loose picks. There are 9 kits, numbered K00-K08. K01 is a client portal. K02 is booking and appointments. K03 is selling a thing with a single seller. K04 is quiz to lead to report. K05 is a membership community. K06 is a breeding and livestock record. K07 is field service and job operations. K08 is own rules and checklists. Each kit names an anchor brick, the main part everything else hangs from.

K00 is different. It is called the floor, and it is forced onto every app. You cannot pick it and you cannot remove it. It holds three bricks: BR-BASICS for sign-in, menus and simple records, BR-TENANCY for keeping each business's data apart, and BR-LEGAL for consent and data protection. Between them they bring seven tables, including tenants, roles, permissions and consents. Because every kit sits on the floor, those three bricks are counted inside every kit, never added on top. K02, for example, has four bricks: the floor's three plus BR-BOOKING.

Here is how it looks for Litterline. It uses K00, the floor, like every app. Its main kit is K06, breeding and livestock record, which brings pedigree, clinical record and breeding events. A pedigree is the record of an animal's parents and ancestors. It adds K08, own rules and checklists, so a breeder can track licence conditions as rows. And it adds K01, the client portal, so puppy buyers can see their own records. Four kits, and a clear list. Trimtable, the grooming desk, picks K00, K02, K01 and K03 instead.

Kits do not stop you adding single bricks. Each kit lists optional members too, such as reminders added to booking to cut no-shows. But the order matters. Start with the floor, choose the kits that match the idea, then add any loose bricks the kits do not cover. This keeps two apps that need the same thing building it the same way, and it means a part proved in one app can be reused in the next. In the next stage you will choose exactly which kits and bricks make the first version. First, a recap.

points: A Brick Is One Reusable Part With An Id
101 Bricks Sit On 8 Colour Spine Shelves
9 Kits K00-K08, With K00 Under Every App
recap.why: Named Kits Turn Loose Wishes Into A Clean List

quiz.why: The registry in use, v0.16, holds 101 bricks.

quiz.why: K00 is the floor: it cannot be picked or removed and sits under every app.

quiz.q: Which three bricks make up K00?
quiz.why: The floor is BR-BASICS, BR-TENANCY and BR-LEGAL, counted inside every kit.

quiz.q: Why does the Body shelf hold the most bricks?
options: Body is the only free shelf
The registry files bot bricks under Body
quiz.why: The registry folds Bots into Body, so bot bricks are counted there.

lessons.title: Choosing Kits And Bricks
lessons.outcome: You can describe how the first version of an app is scoped, mapped and mocked up before Lock.
lessons.body:
Sam was helping to plan Stayproof, our sample inspection pack for boarding kennels. He wanted the first version to do everything a kennel could ever need: daily logs, staff rotas, feeding charts, a shop, reviews, a chat room. Every day the list grew longer, and nothing on it could be built or tested, because nothing was finished. Then someone asked him a different question. What is the smallest app a first customer would pay for and actually use? Everything else could wait on a roadmap. That question is the heart of Stage 3, called Features.

Stage 3 is where the bricks and kits from Stage 2 become a real feature list. It sits in the Research room and it is free. The work is written into a build pack, a set of short notes kept in the app's one document organised by stage, before anything is built. The pack answers five things. Who sees and does what. Which words, labels and colours are data. How payment works. Which tenancy level the app has, using the TEN (0-6) code. And the launch-minimum scope. We will take them one at a time.

The first note is a who-sees-and-does-what map. It has one line for each role and each action. A role is a type of person using the app, such as owner, staff member or customer. A line might say: kennel staff can add a daily log, and only for their own kennel. Each line also names where the check happens on the server side, which means on the computer that holds the data, not just on the screen. A rule that lives only on the screen can be dodged. A rule on the server cannot.

The second note is content as data. Every word, label, colour and category the app shows is listed and stored as rows in a table, never typed into the code. Why bother? Because a reseller app like Litterline wears different brand names. When Northvale Canine Society offers the app to its breeders, the name, colours and wording change, but the layout stays the same. If the words are rows, that swap is an edit to a few rows. If the words are baked into the code, every change becomes a paid building turn.

The third and fourth notes are about money and businesses. The payment route says who takes the money, who is the merchant of record, meaning the business named on the customer's receipt, and how VAT is handled. The PAY (0-2) code helps decide this. The tenancy level uses TEN (0-6), which counts how many businesses share the app and who sits above them. Stayproof is TEN 2: several kennels side by side, none above another. Litterline is TEN 3, because one reseller club sits above its breeders. A higher level needs more walls.

The fifth note is the launch-minimum scope. It is the fewest tables and screens that let a first customer pay and use the app. Everything else goes on the roadmap, which is the list of things to add later. Alongside it sits an in and out list, so everyone can see what was left out on purpose. One checklist rule keeps the scope honest: the first build must fix the three complaints customers mentioned most in research, and include at least one thing no rival has. Small, but already better than what is out there.

Before anything is built, the app gets a clickable mockup. A mockup is a pretend version of the screens you can tap through, with no real data behind it. It is designed phone first, then checked at laptop width, and it follows the house style rules. The mockup also has to use everything in the research: the tables, the rivals, the price range. A mockup made only from colours and calm layouts tends to look nice and say nothing. The person who decides at Lock clicks through it at both widths and says yes.

One more thing goes into Stage 3: a journey map. A journey is one path a person takes through the app, such as signing up, checking an email on another device, signing in, resetting a password or signing out. Each journey is listed and questioned at design time. What does a signed-out visitor see on each page? Does it still work in a new tab? Thinking this through now is free. Finding a broken journey after a paid build is not. Next lesson covers the duties list and the gate that freezes all this. First, a recap.

points: Five Notes Go In The Build Pack Before Lock
Launch-Minimum Means Fewest Screens A Customer Pays For
Clickable Mockup Phone First, Built From The Research
recap.why: Small And Clear Beats Big And Untested

quiz.q: What is the launch-minimum scope?
options: Every feature a customer could ever want
The fewest tables and screens that let a first customer pay and use it
quiz.why: Launch-minimum is the smallest version a first customer would pay for and use; the rest is roadmap.

quiz.q: Why are words, labels and colours stored as data?
options: So a brand swap is an edit to rows, not a paid build turn
So customers can change the code
quiz.why: Rows can be changed per brand without paying for a new building turn.

quiz.q: Where should a who-sees-and-does-what check happen?
options: On the server side, where the data is held
quiz.why: A rule on the server cannot be dodged the way a screen-only rule can.

quiz.q: What must the first build include, by the checklist rule?
options: The top three complaints fixed and one thing no rival has
quiz.why: The feature lock keeps the three most-counted complaints fixed plus one thing no rival has.

lessons.title: Duties And The Lock Gate
lessons.outcome: You can explain the obligations ledger and what must be true before the Lock gate freezes the feature list.
lessons.body:
Ava and her mum were planning Trimtable, our sample booking desk for dog groomers, with a salon called The Tidy Paw in mind. The feature list was short and everyone liked it. They wanted to start building the next morning. Then Ava asked three awkward questions. Who exactly is paying? What does the law ask of an app that stores customers' details? And what is the minimum age to sign up? Nobody knew. The answer was not more features. It was a written list of duties, and one firm decision to freeze the plan.

A duty, or obligation, is something that must exist or be done before a stage or a paid build can go ahead. The factory keeps every known duty in one shared file called OBLIGATIONS.csv. The version in use, v0.6, has 107 rows. Each row says what causes the duty. It might be the build platform itself, which affects every app. It might be one of the codes on the idea card. It might be a brick, or it might be a payment provider, the company that takes card payments. A kit inherits the duties of its bricks.

At Stage 3 the app gets its own obligations ledger, section 3.7 of its document. A ledger is simply a list you keep track of. It is built from the shared file: every platform row, plus the rows for each of the app's codes, plus the rows for each brick it uses, plus the rows for each payment provider it chose. Each row then gets an owner, the gate or prompt it is due by, and a status. When a new duty is learned, from an incident or a refund, a row is added to the shared file in the same turn, so the next app inherits it.

Some rows can only be done by a person, not an agent. Here are examples from the file. Deciding the minimum age and how it is captured, which comes from the BR-LEGAL brick and is due at Lock. Deciding whether one person may hold more than one membership. Ruling on plans and prices before any plan is created. These rows are listed to the person who decides once, as one list with due points. Each then becomes a work item that blocks the gate or prompt it is due at. Agents can draft, but the decision stays with a person.

Here is the rule that gives the ledger its teeth. A gate cannot pass while a ledger row due at that gate is still open or only part done. The same goes for a paid prompt: it cannot even be presented while a row due at it is open. Two automatic checks, called CK50 and CK51, enforce this. So a duty cannot quietly slip past. If the age rule is not decided, Lock does not pass, however good the mockup looks. It sounds strict, and it is. Fixing a missed legal duty after launch costs far more.

The Lock gate sits between Stage 3 and Stage 4, and it has two firm conditions. The first is a named payer: who will pay is written down by name, not assumed. The second is a legal check for this exact scope, because a different scope can bring different law. Trimtable stores customers' names and notes about their dogs, so its SEN (0-3) code is 1, personal data. That brings data protection duties with it. The legal check reads the in and out list and the ledger together, and says whether this version can be built as planned.

Lock is always decided by a person. It never passes automatically. The engine shows one decide row with a plain question: freeze the feature list? There is a reason it is always a person. Lock includes the mockup review, and judging whether a mockup is right is not something a checklist can do. A yes freezes the list. The out list is closed, and anything on it can only come back through a new gate, never by drift. Drift is when extra features creep in a little at a time without anyone deciding.

Lock is also the moment the app is created on the build platform, with its own number and a short web name called a slug. Until now the app was a folder of notes. A live app that wants a new feature later comes back in at Lock too, as a small pack of its own, so every change gets the same check. With the feature list frozen and every duty owned, the next stage can design the tables safely. That is Stage 4, Schema. First, a quick recap of duties and the Lock gate.

points: Every App Gets Its Own Obligations Ledger
Open Duties Due At A Gate Block It
Lock Needs A Named Payer, Legal Check And Yes
recap.why: Freezing The List Stops Drift And Surprise Costs

quiz.q: What is OBLIGATIONS.csv?
options: A shared file of duties keyed to what causes them
quiz.why: It is the shared file of duties, each caused by the platform, a code, a brick or a provider.

quiz.q: What happens when a ledger row due at a gate is still open?
options: The gate passes with a warning
quiz.why: CK50 stops a gate while any row due at it is open or only part done.

quiz.q: Which two conditions does the Lock gate need?
options: A sales page and a domain
A paid prompt and a refund
A named payer and a legal check
quiz.why: Lock needs a named payer and a legal check for the scope.

quiz.q: What happens to the out list after Lock?
options: Its items join automatically next week
It is closed, and items return only through a new gate
quiz.why: The out list closes at Lock; nothing returns by drift.

lessons.title: How The System Makes The Tables
lessons.outcome: You can explain how codes and kits decide the tables, and how each table is built, set and recorded.
lessons.body:
Nia keeps the spreadsheet for her family's walking group, so when she heard Stage 4 was about tables, she thought it would be easy. She planned to add columns as she went, and rename them whenever better names came to mind. Then she learned two facts about the build platform. Renaming a table or column destroys every row in it, and still reports success. And changing who can read a table after it is made costs a paid building turn. So she changed her approach. Plan every table first, set it right at birth, and write down why it exists.

Stage 4 is called Schema. A schema is the plan of the tables that hold the data: which tables exist, which columns each one has, and who may read or write them. A column is one field in a table, like a dog's name or a booking date. Stage 4 sits in the Rig room, together with Stage 5, and it is free. Nothing here is built by the paid builder. The tables are built by hand, then proved by reading them back, which is called a re-read. Free work now saves paid work later.

Where does the list of tables come from? Not from guessing. The kits chosen earlier each bring their own tables. K00, the floor, brings seven: tenants, tenant users, roles, permissions, consents, usage channels and events. K02, booking, adds bookings, availability slots and resources. The codes on the idea card then shape the columns. If TEN (0-6) is 2 or more, several businesses share the app, so every table holding a business's data needs a tenant id column, which says which business owns each row. A tenant is one business using the app.

Before anything is created, the tables and columns are written out as a spec, short for specification, saved as a CSV file. A CSV is a plain file of rows and columns that any program can open. The spec is never left as loose prose, because nobody can test a paragraph. Every name is checked against the naming standard, so one idea always has one name. Then the tables are built by hand, for free, and each one is read back to prove it exists exactly as written. A copied base is also swept for ghost columns, ones it inherited but does not use.

Every table has an access mode, a setting that says who may read and write its rows. Here are some examples. Public means anyone can read, even when signed out. User scoped means each row belongs to the signed-in person who made it. Anonymous writable means a stranger can add rows without signing in. A role gate limits a table to people with a given role, such as staff. The access mode is set when the table is created, which is free. Changing it afterwards is a billed builder turn. So the mode is decided on paper first.

Deciding a mode is not the same as having it. So each table gets an anonymous probe. A probe is a test request, and anonymous means it is sent with nobody signed in, the way a stranger on the internet would arrive. If a table is meant to be private and the probe gets rows back, something is wrong, and it is fixed before going further. The codes set what is allowed. Litterline has POST (0-2) at 0, so no table should take writes from a stranger. VIEW (0-2) at 1 means only link-holders may read anything signed out.

The last piece is the table register, section 4.0 of the app's document. Every table gets one row in it, with the reason the table exists, its role gate and who may write to it. This sounds like paperwork, but it prevents a costly mistake. A table is never removed just because no code seems to read it. Removing a table needs a person's dated ruling. Without a register, a table that looks unused might hold the one record a business needs on inspection day, and deleting it would be very hard to undo.

One rule from the duties file is worth learning by heart. Never rename a table or column. A rename destroys every row and still returns a success message, so nobody notices until the data is gone. If a name must change, the safe way is to add the new column, copy the data across, which is called migrating, and leave the old one unread. Plan, spec, build by hand, set the mode, probe, record. That is how Stage 4 makes its tables. Now a short recap before we meet the walls.

points: Kits Bring The Tables, Codes Shape The Columns
Set Access Mode At Creation, Then Probe Signed Out
Every Table Gets A 4.0 Register Row And Reason
recap.why: Tables Planned Once Are Cheap, Fixed Later Are Not
