quiz.why: A schema is the plan of the tables, their columns and who may read or write them.

quiz.q: Why is the access mode set when a table is created?
options: Because the customer asks for it
Because only resellers can change it
Because setting it then is free and changing it later is a billed turn
quiz.why: Setting the mode at creation is free; changing it afterwards costs a builder turn.

quiz.q: What does an anonymous probe do?
options: Sends a test request with nobody signed in
quiz.why: It checks a table the way a signed-out stranger would reach it.

quiz.q: What is the safe way to change a column name?
options: Add a new column, migrate the data, leave the old one unread
Ask customers to type the data again
quiz.why: A rename destroys every row, so the factory adds, migrates and leaves the old column unread.

lessons.title: Walls And Table Tests
lessons.outcome: You can name the eight walls and describe the table tests that must pass before the Schema gate.
lessons.body:
Theo's cousin works at a grooming salon. One morning, the booking app the salon used showed her another salon's client list, names and phone numbers included. It was fixed within a day, but the trust was gone. When Theo started helping to plan Trimtable, he wanted to be sure it could never do that. At first he wrote, the data is private, in his notes. Then he realised that sentence proved nothing. What he needed was a test for each table that could actually fail, run from outside, with a date beside the result.

In the factory, a wall is a rule that keeps two parties' data apart. The simplest picture has three walls. Owner from owner keeps one reseller's businesses away from another reseller's. Business from business keeps one salon's records away from the next salon's. Customer from customer keeps one customer's details private inside a single business. The third wall always sits inside the second, never instead of it: check the business first, then the customer. Trimtable has no reseller above it, so the first wall has nobody on the other side yet.

The full set has eight walls, numbered W1-W8, and most codes on the idea card point to one. W1 is the brand wall, between businesses. W2 is the member wall, between customers. W3 is the layer-above wall, for parties sitting above a business. W4 is the staff wall, for roles, guests and view-as access. W5 is the membership wall, about who can join and belong, and whose name is shown. W6 is the public wall, for strangers who are signed out. W7 is the data-out wall, for data leaving the app. W8 is the sensitivity hold, for health or children's data.

Stage 4 ends with table tests, section 4.4 of the document. The test depends on the kind of table. Application tables hold a business's own records, like bookings. Each one gets a brand-wall read: sign in as tenant A and try to read tenant B's rows. Tenant A must see none. User tables hold one person's own things. Each one gets a user-wall read: one user must not see another user's rows. Control tables hold the app's own settings, and each gets an anonymous read, sent signed out, which has to return 401.

401 is a status code, a number a web server sends back with every answer. 401 means the request was refused because nobody is signed in. For a control table, that is exactly the answer you want a stranger to get. If the anonymous read returns 200 instead, which means success, and hands back rows, the table is open to the whole internet. That is a stop. The fix comes before anything else, and then the test is run again until it returns 401. A pass is only a pass when the stranger gets nothing.

Some tables are shared on purpose. Imagine one dog's record that two breeders both hold a claim on, with each allowed to see different fields. A field is one column in one row. A shared row carries no tenant id, so a normal row-level test looks for a tenant tag, finds none, and reports all clear, while the wrong fields leak. That is why the rule says a row-level test passes while leaking. On a shared table the leak test must be field-level: check that each claim sees only the fields it is allowed to see.

A test without a result is just a hope. So the stage is finished only when every Launch table and every Base table has at least one test with a dated result. Launch tables are the ones the first version uses. Base tables are the ones that come with the base the app started from. The tests are run from outside, as a real visitor would, not by asking the builder whether it worked. A sentence in the notes, such as the data is private, never counts. Only a test that could fail, and did not, counts.

Then comes the Schema gate. It sits between Stage 4 and Stage 5 and asks: tables probed, names re-read? Like the Base gate, it is automatic. When every Stage 4 checklist line is done, and no section of the document still says pending, the engine moves the app on without anyone clicking yes. That only works because the tests are plain. A probe returned 401 or it did not. A name matches the spec or it does not. Next comes Stage 5, where test businesses and test people are set up. First, the recap.

points: Eight Walls W1-W8 Keep Parties Apart
Brand-Wall, User-Wall And Anonymous 401 Table Tests
Shared Tables Need Field-Level Tests, Then Auto Schema Gate
recap.why: A Test That Can Fail Is The Only Proof

quiz.q: Which wall keeps one business's data away from another business?
quiz.why: W1, the brand wall, sits between businesses.

quiz.q: What should an anonymous read of a control table return?
quiz.why: 401 means the signed-out request was refused, which is the pass.

quiz.q: Why is a row-level test not enough on a shared table?
options: A shared row has no tenant id, so the test can pass while fields leak
quiz.why: On a shared table the leak test must be field-level, because a row-level test passes while leaking.

quiz.q: Who moves the app through the Schema gate?
options: The engine, automatically, when every line is done
quiz.why: Schema is an auto gate: tables probed and names re-read, then the engine moves the app on.

lessons.title: Test Identities And Test Tenants
lessons.outcome: You can explain why every app needs two contrasting test brands and named test members before any paid build starts.
lessons.body:
Meet Sam. He is fourteen, and he was helping to test Trimtable, the booking and client desk for dog groomers. He signed in with his own family account and clicked through every screen. Bookings worked. Client notes saved. He wanted to prove that one grooming salon could never see another salon's clients. But there was a problem he could not get past. There was only one salon in the app, and only one person signed in. Everything looked perfect. Then it clicked. A leak can only show up when there is a second, different business for the data to leak into.

This is Stage 5, called Data. It happens in the room called Rig, the same room where the tables were built by hand in Stage 4. Nothing here costs build credits. Credits are the units the build platform charges each time its AI builder does a piece of work. Stage 5 is the last free stage before the paid one, so it is the place to get ready properly. The job is simple to say: put believable test data into the app, set up test people who can sign in, and write down exactly how the app will be tested before anyone pays for a build.

First, the test tenants. A tenant is one business that uses the app, with its own name and its own data. In this course we also call a tenant a brand. The rule is at least two test tenants, because one tenant cannot prove isolation. Isolation means each brand's data stays behind its own wall. With only one brand, there is nobody for data to leak to, so every test passes and proves nothing. Litterline is sold under the factory's own brand and resold by Northvale Canine Society, so its two test brands mirror that shape.

The two test tenants must be contrasting. That word comes straight from the duty list: the second tenant gets different names, different lanes and different colours, so that a leak is visible. Picture Brand A with green buttons and dogs called Bramble and Pip, and Brand B with orange buttons and dogs called Juniper and Moss. If a Brand B member ever sees the name Bramble, you know at a glance that data has crossed a wall. Seed rows go in at this point too: the starting plans, roles and lists the app needs before anyone signs in.

There is a trap here worth knowing. On the build platform, the preview version of the app and the live version share one database. A database is the store that holds all the tables. So test data is not tucked away in a safe sandbox. It sits right next to real data. The duty list says test rows must be marked and removable, so nobody mistakes them for real customers and they can be cleared before launch. Totals are reconciled as well, and an empty count is written as zero, so nothing is left silently blank.

Next come the test identities. A test identity is a pretend person with a real sign-in, used only for testing. Each brand gets two test members, and each one has its own mailbox. They sign in with an email and password, or with a magic link, which is a one-time sign-in link sent by email. The owner account is kept separate from the test members. All of them are listed in a test identities register in the app's folder: brand, role, email, login type and user id. Passwords are never written in the register.

Two rules sit on top of this. First, no Google single sign-on for test members. Single sign-on is the button that says sign in with Google. It was ruled out after real tests kept signing in the wrong account by itself and signing the editor out. Second, agents never create accounts. The AI helpers in the factory can run tests, but the factory owner sets up the test identities once per app, by hand. Logins live only in the owner's password manager. That way no tool can quietly invent a person or borrow someone's real account.

One last step comes before any build: the new-account walk. A brand-new test account, with its own mailbox, walks the whole journey on the current app, and every break is written down. Why brand-new? Because existing test members already have rows in the tables, and that hides bugs a first-time user would hit straight away. The walk is repeated after every paid turn later on. So, to recap this lesson: two contrasting brands, two named test members for each brand, and a fresh account walk before anyone spends a single credit.

points: Two Contrasting Test Tenants Make A Leak Visible
Two Test Members Per Brand, Each With Own Mailbox
No Google Sign-In, And Agents Never Create Accounts
recap.why: A Test That Cannot Fail Proves Nothing

quiz.q: Why does Stage 5 need at least two test tenants?
options: Two tenants make the app load faster
One tenant cannot prove that data stays behind its wall
The build platform charges less for two tenants
The sales page needs two brand names
quiz.why: With only one brand there is nobody for data to leak to, so every test passes and proves nothing.

quiz.q: What makes the two test tenants contrasting?
options: They use the same colours so tests are fair
They use the same dog names
quiz.why: The duty list asks for different names, lanes and colours so that a leak is visible at a glance.

quiz.q: How do test members sign in?
options: With an email and password or a magic link, each with their own mailbox
With single sign-on through any account
quiz.why: Test members have their own mailboxes and never use Google single sign-on, which signed in the wrong account in real tests.

quiz.q: Who sets up the test identities?
options: An AI agent, during the build
Any test member who needs one
The factory owner, once per app, by hand
quiz.why: Agents never create accounts; the factory owner sets them up once per app and keeps the logins in a password manager.

lessons.title: The Leak And Tenant Tests
lessons.outcome: You can describe a test plan with negative cases, read a test matrix and explain what the Invest gate decides.
lessons.body:
Isla is sixteen. She wrote a checklist to test Stayproof, the inspection pack for boarding kennels, using Hollin Lane Kennels as her example. She wanted proof that each kennel's inspection logs stayed private. Her checklist said things like: a kennel worker can open the daily log, can add a cleaning note, can print the pack. Every line passed. She felt good, until someone asked a simple question. Did you test whether a different kennel can open Hollin Lane's logs? She had not. Her list only tested what should work. The tests that matter most check what must never happen.

In Stage 5 the factory writes a test plan. The rule is one row per test, with its negative case. A positive case checks that something allowed works: a Brand A member can read Brand A's dogs. A negative case checks that something forbidden fails: a Brand B member tries to read Brand A's dogs and gets nothing. Both halves matter. An app that blocks everyone passes every negative case and is useless. An app that lets everyone in passes every positive case and is dangerous. The pair proves the wall is in the right place.

The tests are laid out as a test matrix. A matrix is a grid. Down the side goes every table in the app. Across the top go four kinds of visitor: someone signed out, a Brand A member, a Brand B member, and the owner. Each square says what that visitor should get from that table: everything, their own rows only, or nothing at all. Every table is tested, not only the tables a screen happens to use. Old or forgotten tables are exactly where leaks hide, because nobody is looking at them.

A leak is when someone can see or change data that belongs to somebody else. Brand B reading Brand A's dogs is a leak. A signed-out stranger reading a customer list is a leak. The factory treats a leak as a stop, not as a bug to fix later. The gate rules say leaks are watched throughout the build, and any leak stops the build. Each app carries a leak status on its card. L with a question mark means not tested. Ln means tested, with no leak. Ly means a leak was found.

Here is the clever part. The leak tests are written now, in Stage 5, together with the build prompts, before a single credit is spent. A prompt is the written instruction given to the AI builder. The factory also writes scenario tests in plain prose, which describe a real person's journey step by step, and splits the full prompt sequence into parts. When the paid stage starts, each prompt already has its tests waiting. Nobody has to invent a test after seeing the result, when it is tempting to test only what looks right.

Next, money. The factory estimates how many credits the build will take and writes it on the app's card as the word credits, then a number. The factory owner also sets a credit ceiling, the most this app may spend, and a stop rule. The template gives a default ceiling of 10,000 credits, and says stop at one and a half times the estimate, after two failures, or at 80 percent of the ceiling. A rollback point is saved too: an export ZIP, which is a packed copy of the app's files, with any gaps noted.

Stage 5 ends at the Invest gate, from 5 to 6. Its question is: spend build credits? If the estimate is 1,500 credits or less, and the month's stop line has not been passed, Invest passes by itself. Otherwise the factory owner decides, because this is where real money starts to be spent. Inside Invest sits the Slot check. The factory runs at most three builds at once and always keeps one lane empty for Rescue, for a live app that breaks. If the lanes are full, the app simply waits its turn.

So when Stage 5 closes, the app has two contrasting test brands, named test members, a test plan with a negative case on every row, and a test matrix covering every table for four kinds of visitor. It has a credit estimate, a ceiling, a stop rule and a rollback point. Nothing has been paid for yet. Isla's lesson is the factory's lesson: test what must never happen, write the tests first, and treat any leak as a stop. Next, in Stage 6, the prompts are finally sent to the builder.

points: Every Test Row Carries Its Negative Case
Matrix Covers Every Table For Four Kinds Of Visitor
Invest Passes Itself At 1,500 Credits Or Less
recap.why: Tests Written First Cannot Bend To Fit Results

quiz.q: What is a negative case?
options: A test of the sales page wording
A test that checks something forbidden really fails
A test that is only run on a phone
quiz.why: A negative case proves that something which must never happen, such as Brand B reading Brand A's rows, really does fail.

quiz.q: Which four kinds of visitor does the test matrix cover?
options: Signed out, Brand A member, Brand B member and owner
quiz.why: Every table is checked for a signed-out visitor, a member of each test brand and the owner.

quiz.q: What happens when a leak is found during the build?
options: It is noted for a later version
The leak status stays as not tested
quiz.why: The gate rules say leaks are watched throughout the build and any leak stops the build.

quiz.q: When does the Invest gate pass by itself?
options: When the estimate is 1,500 credits or less and the month's stop line is not passed
Whenever the test plan is written
quiz.why: Invest auto-passes at 1,500 credits or less within the month's stop line; above that, the factory owner decides.

lessons.title: How Build Prompts Are Written
lessons.outcome: You can list what every paid build prompt must carry and explain why each prompt does only one job.
lessons.body:
Rory is thirteen. He was watching his dad plan a change to Trimtable for Juno Platt's salon, The Tidy Paw. Rory had an idea to save time: ask the AI builder to add appointment reminders and a new price list in one request. One message, two jobs, done. His dad shook his head. In this stage every request costs credits, he said, and if a two-job request goes wrong, nobody can tell which half broke, or how to undo just that half. That was the moment it made sense. One prompt, one job, one test, one way back.

This is Stage 6, called Prompts. It happens in the room called Reactor, and it is the only paid stage in the whole factory. Every earlier stage is free planning and free building by hand. Here, the factory sends written instructions, called prompts, to the build platform's AI builder, and each answer, called a turn, spends credits. Because money is spent, the rules get stricter. Every prompt is prepared, checked and tested on paper first, and the factory owner gives the go word before each one is sent. Nothing is sent on a hunch.

The first rule is one goal, one surface. A surface is one part of the app that a person sees or uses, such as the booking screen or the price list. The template line puts it simply: an and means two prompts. Add reminders and change prices is two prompts, not one. Keeping prompts small means a failure is easy to spot and cheap to undo. There is a second split too. Tables and code never go in the same prompt. Tables are made by hand, for free, and the prompt is told not to change them.

Every prompt is built from fixed blocks. A context block lists exactly which files the builder may read, and nothing else. A tables block says the tables were made by hand and must not be changed. And for any app with more than one brand, a walls block goes into every prompt for the life of the app. It states the app's classification, how a row belongs to a tenant, that the app must fail closed, and one line: if a change would weaken this, stop. Fail closed means that when in doubt, the app refuses access.

Each prompt also carries its own test. Where the app has brands, the test covers both walls: the brand wall, where Brand B cannot see Brand A, and the member wall, where one member cannot see another member's rows. The tests are run from outside the app by the factory's agents. The builder is never asked to build test panels or check its own work inside its turn. That would be a bit like marking your own homework. An outside test, run by someone else after the turn, is the only result that counts.

Each paid prompt also carries a written rollback step. Rollback means going back to the last good version if a turn goes wrong. Before sending, the factory takes an export ZIP, a packed copy of every file in the app, so there is always a known good point to return to. Every prompt ends with one fixed line asking the builder, before building, to list anywhere else in the app that must change, and anything this could break. The builder reports that list first. Surprises found before building are cheap. Surprises found after building are expensive.

Before any prompt goes out, the factory writes a three-line pre-send report and adds a task to a list called Sends. Each send moves through fixed steps: draft, check, tested, the go word, sent, and verified live. The go word is a short command the factory owner types to approve one paid send. No agent can give it. Small wording or colour changes skip all of this. They go through the free visual editor instead, never through a paid prompt. Paying credits to change one word would simply be waste.

So a good build prompt is small, tested and reversible. It does one job on one surface. It carries the context block, the tables block and, for any app with brands, the walls block. It brings its own outside test for both walls, a rollback step and the what could this break question. It goes out only after the pre-send report and the owner's go word. Rory's two-job request becomes two careful prompts, each easy to check and easy to undo. Next lesson: what happens the moment a paid turn comes back.

points: One Goal, One Surface: An And Means Two
Walls Block, Test And Rollback In Every Prompt
Owner Gives The Go Word Before Each Paid Send
recap.why: Small Prompts Fail Small And Undo Easily

quiz.q: Why is Stage 6 different from every other stage?
options: It is the only stage with a gate
It is the only stage that uses tables
It is the only stage run by the customer
It is the only stage that spends credits
quiz.why: Stage 6 is the only paid stage; every turn of the AI builder spends credits.

quiz.q: What does the rule 'an and means two prompts' mean?
options: A request with two jobs is split into two prompts
Every prompt must be sent twice
Two people must write each prompt
Each prompt must name two brands
quiz.why: One goal, one surface: if a request needs the word and, it becomes two separate prompts.

quiz.q: What does fail closed mean in the walls block?
options: The app shuts down at night
When in doubt, the app refuses access
The builder closes every file it opens
quiz.why: Failing closed means the safe answer, no access, is the default whenever the app is unsure.

quiz.q: Who runs the tests a prompt carries?
options: The AI builder, inside its own turn
The factory's agents, from outside the app, after the turn
Nobody, the builder's screen is enough
quiz.why: Acceptance tests are run from outside; the builder never builds test panels or checks itself inside its turn.

lessons.title: After Every Paid Turn
lessons.outcome: You can put the six after-turn steps in order and explain what the Send gate needs before an app moves on.
lessons.body:
Ava is fifteen. She watched a Litterline build turn finish. The builder's screen said the new litter page was done, and Ava wanted to message Mara Quill, the breeder waiting for it, straight away. Her mum asked her to wait and run one test first, as a brand-new test member, on the live site. The old page was still showing. The new code had not reached the live app yet. Nothing was broken, but nothing was proved either. Done on the builder's screen is not done. Proved live, from outside, is done.

After every paid turn, the factory follows six steps, always in the same order. One: record the turn. Two: check the spend and look for a refund. Three: publish. Four: re-probe every table. Five: run the member tests. Six: mark the send as done. The order matters. Recording comes first, so nothing is lost if something else goes wrong. Testing comes after publishing, so the tests run on the live app and not on an old copy. The engine refuses to close a send that is missing the record lines.

Step one is record on landing, and it happens before any check, test or reply. The prompt exactly as sent, and the builder's reply, are written down word for word, with the credits and the time. The credit balance is noted on either side of the spend. Cancelled and failed turns are recorded too, because a failure is evidence. Why so strict? Memory is unreliable, and a turn that is not written down cannot be learned from or checked later. Every prompt and its full reply are kept in one file per app.

Step two compares what the turn cost with the written estimate. If it cost more than one and a half times the estimate, the factory stops. It also looks for any charge with no prompt behind it, and for errors on the platform's side that burnt credits. Then it takes a fresh export ZIP and compares the files the prompt named against the last copy. If a named file did not change at all, the turn failed. The rule is to raise a refund ticket, not to send the same prompt again blind.

Step three is publish, which puts the new version on the live site. Before testing, the factory checks that the live site really serves the new code, with the cache defeated. A cache is a saved copy a browser or server keeps so pages load faster, and it can show the old version, just as Ava saw. Step four re-probes every table anonymously. Anonymously means signed out, as a stranger. Every table should refuse a stranger unless it is meant to be public. This anonymous sweep runs after every publish, every time.

Step five is the member tests. After every paid turn, an existing member and a brand-new member of each brand do the app's core action from start to finish. For Litterline, that could mean a breeder adding a litter record. Only the test identities from the register are used, never anyone's own account. After any turn that touched tables or security, the full test matrix runs too: every table, for a signed-out visitor, a Brand A member, a Brand B member and the owner. If a leak appears, the build stops.

Step six marks the send as done, and a scorecard is written: what was predicted against what actually happened. Any gap becomes an action, such as a new checklist line, not just a note. When every planned prompt has been sent and checked, the app reaches the Send gate, from 6 to 7. Its rule is proved live, two fresh sign-ins. Fresh means a new sign-in, not a session left open from earlier. The factory owner decides at this gate. If the answer is yes, the app moves on to Launch.

So here is the lesson in one line: done means proved live from outside. After every paid turn the factory records, checks the spend, publishes, probes every table, runs member tests, and only then closes the send. If a leak was found and fixed, the same turn changes the app's card from Ly to Ln, so the record matches the truth. Ava learned to wait for one test before sending good news. The factory does that on every single turn. Next, the app gets its sales page, its domain and its funnels.

points: Record First, Before Any Check Or Reply
Publish, Then Probe Every Table Signed Out
Send Gate Needs Proof Live And Two Fresh Sign-Ins
recap.why: A Turn Is Only Done When Proved Live

quiz.q: What is the first step after every paid turn?
options: Record the prompt and reply word for word
Tell the customer it is ready
quiz.why: Record on landing comes before any check, test or reply, so nothing is lost.

quiz.q: A file the prompt named did not change after the turn. What does the rule say?
options: Send the same prompt again at once
Ignore it if the screen looks fine
Change the file by hand and move on
The turn failed, so raise a refund ticket and do not resend blind
quiz.why: A named file with no change means the turn failed; the factory raises a refund ticket instead of re-prompting blind.

quiz.q: Why does the factory check the live code before testing?
options: A cache can still be showing the old version
Live code is cheaper to test
Testing before publishing is not allowed by law
quiz.why: A cache keeps saved copies, so tests must confirm the new code is really being served first.

quiz.q: What does the Send gate need before the app moves to Launch?
options: A full month of real users
Proved live, with two fresh sign-ins
quiz.why: The Send gate rule is proved live, two fresh sign-ins, and the factory owner decides.

lessons.title: Sales Page, Domain And Funnels
lessons.outcome: You can explain what a domain, DNS and a funnel are, and why a reseller's brand is never on a free plan.
lessons.body:
Theo is seventeen. He was helping to put together a page for Northvale Canine Society, the club that resells Litterline to its members under its own name. He wanted more club members to try it, so he planned a big button that said free plan. It seemed generous and harmless. But the free plan was refused. Northvale is a reseller, and the factory has a firm rule: a reseller's brand is never on a free plan. That made Theo look much harder at how a button on a page turns into a real, recorded choice.

This is Stage 7, called Launch. It happens in the room called Runway, which is tagged Brand, because this is where the app meets the outside world under each brand's name. The jobs include a sales page, set-up for each brand, the domain, the funnels, and a careful set of launch tests. This lesson covers the outside pieces: the page people land on, the web address they type, and the path that leads them from a first look to signing up. The next lesson covers the launch tests and the Launch gate.

The sales page explains what the app does, who it is for and what it costs. The template line asks for three things: the sales page, a rival line and a launch price. A rival line is a short, honest statement of how this app differs from what people use now. The factory drafts the page, and the factory owner approves it. Much of the wording comes from the research in Stage 1, where customers' own words about their problem were collected. People trust words that sound like their own experience.

A domain is the name of a website, the words people type to find it. Computers find each other by number, so the internet keeps an address book called DNS, the Domain Name System. DNS records point the name at the server where the app lives. The factory picks the domain name in Stage 3, then buys it and sets the records in Stage 4: one for the bare name and one for the www version. SSL, the padlock in the browser that keeps traffic private, is set up too. In Stage 7, all three are verified from outside.

A funnel is a short series of pages that leads a visitor from a first look to signing up or paying. It is wide at the top, where many people arrive, and narrow at the bottom, where fewer people act. The factory builds its landing page and funnel in ClickFunnels, a tool for making sales pages and funnels. The offer was first drafted back in Stage 1 in a funnel shape: who the customer is, the hook, which is their problem in their own words, and the offer itself. That same page is used again here.

How does ClickFunnels talk to the app? The simplest route is a built-in connection that sends sign-ups and tags across. A tag is a label on a contact, such as trial started. One security rule matters a lot: never unlock paid content using a tag that public code can apply, because any visitor could apply it. Another rule: never store a ClickFunnels key or password in the app's database. The app stores only which brand links to which workspace. Paid access is decided by the app itself, never by a label.

Now the plan. Each button on a landing page carries both the brand and the plan inside its link. The plan travels through sign-in the same way the brand does. The rule is sign in first, pay second. When the person comes back, the server checks the plan really is one of that brand's offers, records the chosen plan against the member even if they abandon checkout, and opens that plan's checkout. The price is never taken from the web address, because anyone can edit a web address. Each payment is stamped with the buyer's brand.

Free is decided per brand offer, never for the whole app. The factory owner's own brands may offer a free plan. A reseller's brand never has a free offer. So when Theo's button asked for a free plan on Northvale's brand, the server refused it, exactly as designed. Northvale's members go from sign-in straight to the pay page, then on to their dashboard. To sum up: a sales page the owner approves, a domain proved from outside, funnels in ClickFunnels, and a plan that travels safely with every click.

points: DNS Points The Domain At The App
The Link Carries Brand And Plan, Never Price
A Reseller Brand Is Never On A Free Plan
recap.why: Every Click Must Land On A Recorded, Checked Plan

quiz.q: What does DNS do?
options: It points a domain name at the server where the app lives
It tests every table for leaks
quiz.why: DNS is the internet's address book: its records point a name people can type at the server that holds the app.

quiz.q: What does a landing page button carry inside its link?
quiz.why: The link carries brand and plan; the server then checks the plan is one of that brand's offers.

quiz.q: Why is the price never taken from the web address?
options: Anyone can edit a web address
quiz.why: A visitor could change the address, so the server looks up the real price from the brand's own offers.

quiz.q: Which brands may offer a free plan?
options: The factory owner's own brands, never a reseller's
quiz.why: Free is set per brand offer; the owner's brands may offer it, but a reseller brand is never on a free plan.

lessons.title: The Launch Walk And Boosts
lessons.outcome: You can name the checks that come before the Launch gate and explain why the weekly boost is still only proposed.
lessons.body:
Maya is twelve. She tried the new Stayproof site on her laptop, signing up as a brand-new kennel worker, and everything worked. She was ready to say it could launch. Then she tried again on her phone. The sign-up email arrived, she tapped the link, and the page that opened had forgotten who she was. On the laptop, she had opened the email link in the same browser. On the phone, it opened somewhere new. Launch tests have to walk the whole journey, as a brand-new person, on desktop and on phone.

Before launch, the leak check runs one last time, and it is strict. Every table is tested, with negative cases, using two accounts. Not only the tables a screen happens to use, but every one, including old and forgotten ones. A negative case, as you know, checks that something forbidden really fails. The result sets the app's leak status: Ln for tested with no leak, or Ly for a leak found. An app showing Ly does not launch. In the factory's gate set, Leak is a check inside the Launch gate, not a separate gate.

Next comes the launch walk. Before the gate, a brand-new account for each brand walks the whole journey on the live site, on desktop and on phone, including email links opened on the phone. The journey map is the list of every step a person takes, from the first page to the app's core action, and it includes steps the factory does not build itself, like the sign-up email. Maya's phone problem is exactly what this walk is there to catch. An onboarding walk for each type of user follows the same idea.

Then comes the user-switch test, a standard check on every app. In one browser, sign in as user A and set a display name. Sign out. Sign in as user B. User B must see none of user A's name, footer text or settings. This catches a sneaky kind of leak, where the browser remembers something from the last person. On a shared family computer, or a laptop on a kennel's front desk, that really matters. It sounds simple, and it is, but real apps have failed this test more than once.

Money is tested for real. Checkout is tested on the live link with a 100 percent off test code: buy, sign in, and get access. Checkout never works in preview, so it has to be the live link. A real payment and a refund are also run from start to finish. Around this sit other duties due before launch: legal and consent pages live, with the marketing box left unticked, a security review before publishing, and proof that a user can delete their account and export their data, and that both actually work.

The support route is tested too, so a real person with a problem can actually reach help. Then comes the Launch gate, from 7 to 8. Its question is: open it to real users? The factory owner always decides this one. There is no auto-pass here. The engine describes it as Leak, Launch and Live in one move: the leak check passed, the launch walk done, and the first real user proved from start to finish. After a yes, the app leaves the build board and appears only in Operate.

What about growing the app after launch? The factory's template has a weekly boost line: a weekly proposal of ways to help the app get found, using parts from the Boost shelf, such as public pages, reviews, search visibility and funnels. But be clear about its status. The weekly boost is marked PROPOSED. It sits in the template as an idea that has not been ruled on, so this course teaches it as a proposal, not as a rule. In the factory, a proposal counts for nothing until the live system actually does it.

So before an app opens to real users, it passes a leak test on every table with two accounts, a launch walk on desktop and phone, a user-switch test, a live checkout test, legal and consent checks and a tested support route. Then the factory owner says yes at the Launch gate. Scheduled jobs switch on: the leak probe, the backup and the credit watch. Maya's phone found a real gap, and now the walk finds that kind of gap every time. Next module: how a live app is watched every single day.

points: Leak Test Every Table With Two Accounts
Walk The Journey New, On Desktop And Phone
The Owner Always Decides The Launch Gate (7-8)
recap.why: Real Users Deserve An App Proved On Every Path

quiz.q: Why does the launch walk include a phone?
options: Phones are faster to test on
The sales page is only shown on phones
Email links opened on a phone can break a journey that works on desktop
quiz.why: The walk covers desktop and phone, including email links opened on the phone, because journeys can break between devices.

quiz.q: What does the user-switch test check?
options: That two users can share one account
That user B sees none of user A's name or settings in the same browser
That users can switch brands freely
That the owner can sign in as anyone
quiz.why: Signing in as A, then out, then in as B in one browser shows whether anything of A's is left behind.

quiz.q: Why is checkout tested on the live link?
options: The live link is free to use
The test code only works on phones
quiz.why: Checkout does not work in preview, so the 100 percent off test code is used on the live link.

quiz.q: What is the status of the weekly boost?
options: A gate the owner must pass
A rule that runs every day
quiz.why: The weekly boost line is marked PROPOSED, so it is taught as an idea, not a rule.

lessons.title: Watching A Live App Daily
lessons.outcome: You can explain the daily, weekly and monthly checks that watch a live app, and when each one runs.
lessons.body:
Isla spent weeks helping a team launch Litterline, the licence and records hub for dog breeders. On launch day she thought the hard part was over and she could move on to the next idea. Then one question kept nagging at her. If a change went wrong overnight, and one breeder could suddenly see another breeder's puppy buyers, who would notice? Nobody was sitting up watching. Her answer arrived the next morning, at twenty to seven. The factory had already checked every table by itself. Launch is not the end of the road. It is the start of a lap.

Stage 8 is Operate, and its room is called Radar. A room is simply a place on the factory floor where apps at one stage sit. Radar's tag is Watching, because watching is the main job here. A live app is serving real people, so it cannot be pulled back to an earlier stage like a draft. Instead it goes round a lap. Every fix and every new feature re-enters the road part-way, and the only way out is a gate called Retire. So Stage 8 has no gate out. It has a set of checks that run again and again.

Behind the factory sits the engine. The engine is a script, which means a small program that runs on a timer and does the same job the same way each time. Every 15 minutes it reads the task board, where each app has one card showing its stage, and writes a state file. A state file is a plain record of where every app is right now. The factory dashboard reads that file, so the picture on screen is never more than about 15 minutes old. Nobody has to update it by hand, and nobody can quietly forget.

The most important morning job is the leak probe, at 06:40 UK time. A leak is when data crosses a wall it should never cross, such as one breeder seeing another breeder's records, or a stranger reading something without signing in. A table is one list of records, like a single tab in a spreadsheet. The probe asks each live table for data while signed out, and checks what comes back. For private data the right answer is a refusal. If anything comes back that should not, the probe raises an incident, which is a recorded problem, dated and tagged to the app.

The leak probe has neighbours on the clock. At 06:10 UK time a stale check looks for tasks that have stopped moving. At 07:30 on weekdays a daily digest gathers what changed into one short summary for the owner. Every Monday at 05:20 a weekly backup runs, and the same job runs a change watch, which looks for changes on the platform the apps are built on. There is also a credit watch. Credits are the units the building platform charges for paid work, so the factory keeps a running eye on how many are being spent.

When an app goes live, it joins the weekly security check. That check covers three things for each app: its live links, its sign-in and its leak probe. A dead link, or a sign-in page that no longer works, is just as real a problem as a leak, because people cannot use the app. Each week the app also gets an export, which is a full copy of the app saved as a file, plus a backup of its records. The link to the backup folder is written on the app's card, so a restore never starts with a search.

Some checks run once a month. The app's KPIs, short for key performance indicators, are compared with the targets set for it. A KPI is simply a number you agreed to watch, such as how many breeders signed in this month. There is also a quieter job called new parts back to bricks, which is rule R14. If building the app created a useful new part, that part goes back into the brick registry, the factory's list of reusable parts. The next app can then start from it, instead of building the same thing twice.

Notice who does the watching. Scripts and AI helpers run the probes, the backups and the counts, and they record every result so it can be proved later. They never change who can see what. That decision stays with a person. One more weekly job is marked PROPOSED, which means it has been suggested but is not switched on yet: a weekly boost proposal, an idea for one small change to help people find the app. So the lap is watched by machines and steered by people. Let's recap what watches a live app, and when.

points: Leak Probe Runs Daily At 06:40 UK Time
Weekly Security Check: Live Pages, Sign-In, Leak Probe
Engine Refreshes The Picture Every 15 Minutes
recap.why: A Live App Serves Real People Every Single Day

quiz.q: At what time does the daily leak probe run?
quiz.why: The leak probe runs every morning at 06:40 UK time, after the stale check at 06:10.

quiz.q: What does the weekly security check cover for each live app?
options: Live links, sign-in and the leak probe
quiz.why: A live app joins the weekly security check for its links, its sign-in and its leak probe.

quiz.q: When the probe asks a private table for data while signed out, what is the right answer?
quiz.why: Private data must refuse a signed-out request; anything else is a leak and raises an incident.

quiz.q: What does rule R14 ask for after an app ships?
options: New parts go back to the brick registry
quiz.why: R14 sends useful new parts back to the bricks so the next app can reuse them.

lessons.title: The Money Line
lessons.outcome: You can read a monthly money line and explain when the Return rule and the Retire question come in.
lessons.body:
Sam looked after the numbers for Trimtable, the booking and client desk built for groomer Juno Platt at The Tidy Paw. Juno asked him a simple question: is the app worth keeping? Sam had pages of reports, charts of sign-ins and lists of bookings, and he still could not give her a straight answer. Every chart told a slightly different story. Then he saw how the factory does it. It asks for one line a month: what came in and what went out. That single line, written the same way every month, is enough to raise the right question at the right time.

This is called the money line. It is written on the app's card, which is the one home of the app's facts, and it follows a fixed pattern. It starts with the word money, then the year and the month, then the word in followed by the pounds that came in, then the word out followed by the pounds that went out. For example: money, September 2026, in X, out Y. Because the pattern never changes, a script can read it without guessing. Many months of lines, one under another, become a simple history of the app.

Who writes the money line? Not a script and not an AI helper. On the factory's stage 8 checklist it is tagged as the owner's own work, so a person writes it each month. That makes sense. Money facts live in bank statements, platform bills and payment reports, and a person who can see all of them is best placed to sum them honestly. The scripts then do what scripts are good at: they read the line, compare it with earlier months and raise a flag when a pattern appears. The person supplies the truth, the machine watches it.

Let's read one. These numbers are invented for teaching. Suppose Trimtable's line says in 90, out 140. More went out than came in, so that is a losing month. On its own, one losing month is information, not a verdict. Perhaps a yearly platform bill landed that month, or bookings dipped during a holiday. Nothing happens automatically after one losing month. The line simply sits on the card for anyone to see. The factory is not asking whether a single month was good. It is watching for a pattern that keeps going.

Here is the pattern it watches for. If the money line shows two losing months running, the engine asks the Retire question. Retire is a gate, and its question is: switch it off and archive it? The question appears as one row on the decide list, which is the short list of things waiting for a person's yes or no. The question can also be raised by hand, if someone tags the app with retire-ask. Asking is not deciding. A person reads the facts and chooses. This two-month rule was added on 20 Oct 2026.

There is a second money rule, called Return, ruling R02. Remember the Invest gate, where build credits are spent on paid work. Return says: no new Invest for an app until it has earned back its credits, or 90 days of use show it will. So if Juno wants a new feature for Trimtable, the factory first asks whether the app has paid back what it already cost to build. Return does not switch anything off. It guards the next spend, so money is not poured into an app that has not yet shown it can stand up.

Return is not automated yet. It is a line on the stage 8 checklist, done by an AI helper and answered with a dated note in the app's document, in the part about payoff. The rule books also tie the lap to Return, while the engine uses the two losing months rule for Retire. The course teaches both, because they do different jobs. Two losing months raises the question of switching off. Return decides whether more credits may be spent. Where the files differ, the course follows what the engine does today.

One last point matters a great deal. The money line is a record of what happened, never a forecast of what will happen. Nothing in this course promises that any app will make money, and every figure in this lesson is invented. Some apps earn back their cost and some do not, and the factory is built to notice either outcome early and honestly. That is why the line is short, monthly and written by a person. It keeps the decision clear and keeps hope out of the sums. Let's recap the money line.

points: Money Line Each Month: In X Out Y
Two Losing Months Running Asks The Retire Question
Return R02 Guards The Next Invest
recap.why: One Honest Line Beats A Pile Of Charts

quiz.q: What does the monthly money line record?
quiz.why: The money line records the pounds that came in and went out that month, on the app's card.

quiz.q: What happens after two losing months running?
options: The app is deleted at once
A person is asked the Retire question
quiz.why: The engine asks a person whether to switch the app off and archive it; asking is not deciding.

quiz.q: What does the Return rule R02 say?
options: No new Invest until the app earns back its credits, or 90 days of use show it will
Every app must make money in its first week
Apps return to stage 0 each year
quiz.why: Return guards the next spend: no new Invest until the credits are earned back or 90 days show they will be.

quiz.q: Who writes the monthly money line?
options: A visitor to the sales page
A person, as named work on the checklist
quiz.why: The money line is tagged as the owner's own work, so a person writes it and scripts read it.

lessons.title: Rescue, Retire And Recycle
lessons.outcome: You can follow a live app through Rescue, Back to Operate, Retire, Recycle, Recovery and Re-imagine.
lessons.body:
Rory kept an eye on Stayproof, the inspection pack used by Hollin Lane Kennels. One morning the leak probe raised an incident against it. Rory's first thought was speed: fix it now, before anyone notices. His second thought was worry. Rushing a fix felt like the surest way to skip a check and break something else. Then he learned how the factory handles trouble. It keeps one build lane empty, just for rescues. The fix is fast because the way is already clear, not because any step is skipped. Let's follow Stayproof round the rescue lap.

Three gates belong to the lap rather than the road: Trouble, Back to Operate and Retire. Trouble comes first, and it is automatic. When an open incident is tagged to a stage 8 app, the engine moves that app to the Rescue room at its next refresh, within about 15 minutes. Rescue's tag is Urgent. The rule books call this a detection, not a judgement. Nobody votes on whether a leak is serious enough. The app simply leaves the healthy list, and the person who owns the factory is told straight away.

The fix re-enters the road at the Slot check, which sits inside the Invest gate. Slot allows at most 3 builds at once, with 1 lane always kept for rescue, so a rescue never waits in a queue. The fix is capped to the break. That means it repairs only what broke. Anything else the fix might touch becomes a roadmap item, a planned change for later, which comes back through the Lock gate as a small pack of its own. A rescue skips Merit and Lock, because the live app has already proved it is worth having.

Fast does not mean unchecked. A person still approves the sending of every paid build prompt, exactly as in Stage 6. The speed comes from the empty lane, never from going round the person. After the fix is sent, the result has to be proved live from outside, with the cache defeated. A cache is a saved older copy of a page that a browser or server may show instead of the newest one. Defeating it means making sure you are testing the real, current app, not a memory of yesterday's.

Once no incident is open, the engine puts one question to a person, and this is the Back to Operate gate: is the fix proved live? A yes moves Stayproof out of Rescue and back to Radar, where the daily checks carry on as before. One detail is worth knowing. A ruling says rescue should be possible from any stage, not just for live apps. That rule is still only PROPOSED. Today the engine rescues stage 8 apps only, and the course teaches what the engine does today.

Retire is the last lap gate, and the only way an app ever leaves the factory. It is asked after two losing months running, or when someone tags the app retire-ask. The person deciding looks at the app's own row: what it costs to keep, who still uses it, and when it was last opened. A yes sets the app's status to RETIRED. Customers are told and the hosting is switched off. Whether retiring also exports or erases the app's data is a ruling that has not been settled yet.

Retiring is not throwing away. Next comes Recycle, whose room is tagged Parts Back. The retired app's bricks, its kits and any proved formation go back to the Reserve room, where parts wait to be used again. A formation is a group of bricks that has been proved to work well together. The app's id, its row and its card are kept for ever. An app is never renamed or wiped from the record. Years later, someone can still see what it was, what it was built from and why it stopped.

Not every idea reaches the lap. If an idea is killed before any parts exist, for example at the Screen gate, it goes to the Recovery room, tagged Killed Or Held. Its id is called burnt, which means it is used up, yet the idea can still be brought back out later if things change. Recycle never applies at the Merit gate, because at that point there are no built parts to give back. Recovery keeps the idea and the reasons it stopped, so nobody pays to research the same dead end twice.

There is one more move, called Re-imagine. It is a door, not a stamp, meaning nobody has to approve a gate to open it. Re-imagine keeps an app's assembly, the way its parts fit together, and points it at a new audience under a new id. Stayproof's inspection pack, for instance, could be re-imagined for a different kind of animal business. A clone like that is paid work, so it goes through the Invest gate like any build. Nothing is wasted and nothing is skipped. Let's recap the lap.

points: Trouble Gate Moves A Broken App To Rescue
Retire Is The Only Way Out; A Person Decides
Parts Go To Reserve; Killed Ideas Go To Recovery
recap.why: Fast Fixes And Clean Endings Keep The Factory Honest

quiz.q: What moves a live app into Rescue?
options: An open incident tagged to the app
quiz.why: The Trouble gate is automatic: an open incident on a stage 8 app moves it to Rescue at the next refresh.

quiz.q: Why can a rescue fix move quickly?
options: One build lane is always kept empty for rescue
quiz.why: Slot keeps 1 of its 3 lanes for rescue, so the fix never queues; the approvals and tests still happen.

quiz.q: Where do a retired app's bricks, kits and proved formations go?
quiz.why: Recycle sends the parts of a retired app back to the Reserve room to be used again.

quiz.q: What does Re-imagine do?
options: Deletes the app and its row
Points the same assembly at a new audience under a new id
Moves the app back to stage 0
quiz.why: Re-imagine keeps the assembly, gives it a new id and audience, and the paid clone goes through Invest.

lessons.title: Filling In Your First Idea Form
lessons.outcome: You can fill in an idea form, using the fictional Litterline as a worked example.
lessons.body:
Ava had followed the whole course, and she had an app idea of her own written on a sticky note by her desk. She wanted to send it into the factory properly, the way a real idea goes in. Then she opened the form, saw the 20 codes and froze. It felt like a test she might fail. What helped was watching someone fill in a finished example first. The codes turned out to be plain questions about who signs in and what they see, and most of them allow the answer not yet known. So let's fill one in together.

Every idea enters the factory through one of four doors. The first is the owner's own idea form. Two more are internal doors for ideas the factory finds by itself, including ideas suggested by AI. The fourth is a door for clients, meaning people outside the factory, and that door is not built yet. Whichever door an idea uses, it lands in the same place: Reception, the room for Stage 0, tagged Free, because nothing is spent here. Our worked example is Litterline, a fictional app, so every name and number you hear is invented.

The form starts with a short name: Litterline. Then comes the brief, which is three plain answers. What is it? A licence and records hub for dog breeders. Who pays? Breeders, and clubs that resell it under their own name, such as the fictional Northvale Canine Society. What is the pain? Licence renewals mean weeks of hunting through paper. The form also notes the rule behind the idea, here the dog breeding licence rules in England and Wales. A good brief is short enough to say in one breath, and specific enough that a stranger could picture the customer.

Now the 20 codes, in four groups. Each code is a word plus a number. Six are required: TEN, CUST, SEN, VIEW, POST and PAY. The other 14 may say not yet known. Group 1 is Businesses. TEN (0-6) is 3, one reseller above, because the club sits above its breeders. PARENTS (0-3) is 1, so each breeder sits under one party. DOWN (0-3) is 1: the club can read the layer below. MEET (0-3) is 0, so breeders never meet each other. POOL (0-3) is 1, only when enough contribute. EXIT (0-3) is 2: a leaving breeder's data is handed to them.

Group 2 is Who Signs In. ROLE (0-2) is 2, roles with different access, so a breeder and their helper need not see the same things. BELONG (0-2) is 1: each person belongs to one business. GUEST (0-1) is 1, which means a business can let an outside person in with a scoped view, a narrow window onto only what they need. HELP (0-3) is 1: the owner can view the app as another person sees it, view only, and every look is logged. JOIN (0-2) is 1, so accounts are created through a brand address or a join link, not by anyone at all.

Group 3 is Customers. CUST (0-5) is 3, customers write, so puppy buyers can add to their records. PRICE (0-3) is 1, one price list. SHARE (0-1) is 0: members do not share with each other. SEN (0-3) is 1, personal data, but nothing health-related or about children. Group 4 is Public. VIEW (0-2) is 1, so only people holding a link can read while signed out. POST (0-2) is 0: strangers cannot put data in. BRAND (0-2) is 2, a brand per business. SEND (0-2) is 1, users download their own data. PAY (0-2) is 2: payouts within one chain.

Next come the three kill questions. FRAGILE: could it give wrong answers that look right? ONESHOT: would people use it once and stop? NOHOOK: is there no reason to come back? In our worked example all three are answered no, partly because licences renew, which brings breeders back. With no kill answer and SEN below 2, the engine suggests the verdict PASS. It also suggests a data role, such as CONTROLLER, PROCESSOR, BOTH or NONE, and a person confirms it. Then the Screen gate asks a person one question: start work on this idea?

Your turn. Take your own idea and write a short name, then the three-part brief: what it is, who pays, and the pain it removes. Answer the six required codes first, TEN, CUST, SEN, VIEW, POST and PAY, and write not yet known wherever you honestly are not sure. That is allowed, and it is better than a guess. Your answers become the app's card, its one home, which is never overwritten; changes become a new version. The link to a client idea form is marked TO CONFIRM, because that door is still being built. Let's recap.

points: Brief Is Three Answers: What, Who Pays, Pain
Six Codes Required, Fourteen May Say Not Yet Known
No Kill Answer And SEN Below 2 Means PASS
recap.why: A Clear Form Gives Your Idea A Fair Hearing

quiz.q: Which three answers make up the brief?
options: What it is, who pays, and the pain
quiz.why: The brief is what it is, who pays, and the pain it removes, said in plain words.

quiz.q: Litterline is TEN 3. What does level 3 mean?
quiz.why: TEN (0-6) level 3 means one reseller above the businesses, like a club above its breeders.

quiz.q: How many of the 20 codes are required?
quiz.why: TEN, CUST, SEN, VIEW, POST and PAY are required; the other 14 may say not yet known.

quiz.q: Litterline has no kill answers and SEN 1. Which verdict does the engine suggest?
quiz.why: No kill answer and SEN below 2 gives PASS; SEN 2-3 would give HOLD.

lessons.title: Where To Go Next
lessons.outcome: You can describe the Vision 2029 picture and the honest next steps on the value ladder.
lessons.body:
Leah finished the course with one idea form filled in, and she wanted to know what could come after a single idea. So she searched online, and everything she found promised apps that make money while you sleep. She trusted none of it, and she was right not to. What she needed was an honest picture: where the factory is heading, what the next steps are, and what nobody can promise. That picture turned out to be calmer and more useful. It is a road of clear steps, with a person deciding at the gates.

First, the future. Everything in the next two parts is Vision 2029, illustrative. That means it is a picture of what the factory aims to look like, drawn to show scale. It is not today's numbers and it is not a forecast. In this picture there are about 1,000 live apps, and one new app arrives each day. Every figure you hear is invented to make the idea concrete. Holding a clear picture helps the factory build the right checks now, because a check that works for one app has to work for a thousand.

Still Vision 2029, illustrative. Imagine 06:40 UK time. The leak probe reports All Clear across 18,240 tables. Three apps sit in the Rescue room, each with one capped fix moving through the lane kept empty for trouble. Two hundred and twelve apps have been retired, with their parts back in Reserve. The decide list, where a person answers yes or no, is capped at 10 rows, and 7 are open. Notice what scale does not change. The same probe, the same money line and the same gates you learned in this course run for every app.

Even in the vision, automation does the checking and the carrying between gates, and a person still decides at the human gates. Those are Screen, Merit, Lock, Invest unless it passes automatically at 1,500 credits or less, Send, Launch, Back to Operate and Retire. On the full flow map of the future factory, a person appears only at those points. That is the design, not a weakness. Machines are good at doing the same check a thousand times. People are needed where judgement, money and law meet, and that does not change with scale.

Now the next steps. A value ladder is a set of steps, where each step offers a little more help for the people who want it, and nobody has to climb higher than suits them. The App Factory ladder has five steps. One, this course, which teaches the road. Two, the idea form, where you send in your own idea. Three, an app built for you through the stages. Four, a reseller plan, where a business puts its own name on an app. Five, a partner link. Let's take them in pairs.

Step one is where you are now. The course explains how an idea becomes a live app: stages, rooms, gates, codes, bricks, walls and tests, in plain words. Step two is the idea form. A client door into the factory is being built, so the link is marked TO CONFIRM until it exists. When it opens, you would answer the same plain questions you practised with Litterline: what it is, who pays, the pain, and the required codes. A person then decides at the Screen gate whether work starts, exactly as you learned.

Step three is an app built for you, through the same stages and gates. Step four is a reseller plan. A reseller is a business that sells an app under its own name, the way the fictional Northvale Canine Society could offer Litterline to its breeders. One rule is firm: a reseller brand is never on a free plan. Members sign in first and pay second. The plan they chose on the landing page travels with them, is recorded, and is checked against that brand's offers. The price is never taken from the web address.

Step five is a partner link for the platform the factory builds on. That link is marked TO CONFIRM, because it is not set yet. And here is the most important line in this lesson. There are no income promises anywhere in this course. Results depend on your own work, and nothing here says that any app, plan or link will make money. What the course can promise is understanding: how real apps are planned, checked and run, and the questions to ask before any money is spent. Let's recap where to go next.

points: Future Figures Are Always Vision 2029, Illustrative
People Still Decide At The Human Gates
A Reseller Brand Is Never On A Free Plan
recap.why: Honest Steps Matter More Than Big Promises

quiz.q: What must every figure about the future carry in this course?
quiz.why: Future figures, such as about 1,000 apps or one a day, are always marked Vision 2029, illustrative.

quiz.q: In the Vision 2029 picture, who decides at the human gates?
